native_result.query: In which years were individuals with a criminal record found to have significantly lower wealth compared to those without?
native_result.HypoA: In 1985, 1990, and 1996, individuals with a criminal record have significantly lower wealth compared to those without.
native_result.HypoB:
Hypothesis: In 1985, 1990, and 1996 — the three wealth-survey years available in this dataset — individuals who had ever been jailed between 1985 and 1994 (ever_jailed == 1, n = 289) had significantly lower composite wealth than those who had not (n = 11,724), after applying Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction at alpha = 0.05 across the three year-tests. Both sensitivity analyses (Mann-Whitney U; Welch t on log1p(wealth − min + 1)) agree on direction and significance at every year, so the primary answer set is {1985, 1990, 1996}.

Secondary characterisation (recorded in the workflow only, not the answer set): the largest raw-dollar gap between groups is in 1996 (mean difference ≈ $85,063), followed by 1990 (≈ $57,598) and 1985 (≈ $17,157), reflecting a divergence that widens across the three wealth snapshots.

Boundary statement (recorded per U1 and per the dataset scope): because the dataset only carries wealth columns for 1985, 1990, and 1996, the hypothesis is restricted to those three years; years such as 1979, 2000, and 2002 cannot be evaluated. Because ever_jailed is defined for the 1985–1994 window and composite_wealth_1985 is measured at the start of that window, the 1985 comparison is contemporaneous with the exposure window rather than strictly pre-dating it; the cross-sectional "criminal-record group has lower wealth" comparison is therefore descriptive of group differences at each measured year rather than a clean pre/post causal contrast.
